questions.question: What is the practical meaning of calling a vector space finite-dimensional?
options: It can be generated by finitely many vectors.
It contains only finitely many distinct vectors.
Each vector is a finite combination of some vectors.
Its vectors are lists with finitely many entries.

questions.question: Does finite-dimensional mean that the vector space has finitely many vectors?
options: Yes; finitely many spanning vectors give finitely many sums.
No; $\mathbb{R}^2$ has infinitely many vectors but dimension $2$.
Yes; dimension $n$ means the space holds exactly $n$ vectors.
No; it means each vector has finitely many nonzero entries.

questions.question: Why can a spanning list be longer than the dimension of the space?
options: Because dimension is the length of the longest spanning list.
Because a basis only has to span, not be independent.
Because a spanning list may contain redundant vectors.
Because the dimension changes with the spanning list chosen.

questions.question: What does finite-dimensionality allow us to do with vector-representation problems?
options: Reduce to finitely many basis coefficients.
Write each vector as a multiple of one basis vector.
Use coefficients that do not depend on the basis.
Check only finitely many vectors in the space.

questions.question: Does a finite-dimensional vector space have to come from geometry such as $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: Yes; spaces of polynomials are always infinite-dimensional.
No; polynomials of degree at most $2$ also form an example.
Yes; only Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{R}^n$ can be finite-dimensional.
No, but other examples must contain finitely many vectors.

questions.question: If $V=\operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, which conclusion is justified?
options: $V$ has dimension exactly $3$.
$V$ contains exactly $3$ vectors.
$V$ has no basis because the list might be redundant.
$V$ is finite-dimensional, with dimension at most $3$.

questions.question: If a vector space has a basis of length $5$, what follows?
options: Every spanning list of it has exactly five vectors.
It contains exactly five vectors, the basis ones.
It must be $\mathbb{R}^5$ with the standard basis.
It is finite-dimensional of dimension $5$.

questions.question: Why is $\mathbb{R}^n$ finite-dimensional?
options: Each of its vectors has finitely many nonzero entries.
Every vector in it is a multiple of one fixed vector.
It contains just $n$ vectors, namely the standard ones.
Spanned by the $n$ standard coordinate vectors.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ the list $((1,0),(0,1),(1,1))$ spans the space. What is true about writing $(2,3)$ as a linear combination of this list?
options: It can be written in more than one way, since the list is linearly dependent.
It can be written in exactly one way, since the list spans $\mathbb{R}^2$.
It cannot be written, since a spanning list of $\mathbb{R}^2$ has two vectors.
It can be written only with coefficient $0$ on the vector $(1,1)$.

questions.question: Why is the space $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$ of all real polynomials, of any degree, infinite-dimensional?
options: A finite list has degrees at most some $d$, so $x^{d+1}$ is never in its span.
It contains infinitely many polynomials, so no finite list can list them all.
Its elements are functions, not lists of real numbers.
Adding polynomials can raise the degree beyond every bound.
